Indian defending champion D Gukesh competes against Uzbekistan's challenger Javokhir Sindarov during the first game of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026, in Geneva, Switzerland.

Playing with white for the first time in the match, Gukesh opened with the London System, possibly looking for a more cautious approach after facing pressure in the opening game, where Sindarov had pushed for an advantage but could not convert it.However, Sindarov was able to equalise through a series of straightforward moves, leaving little room for either player to gain an edge in the middle game.

WyXFJIQZ.description: Reigning champion D Gukesh drew Uzbekistan's Javokhir Sindarov in 20 moves with white on Wednesday, leaving the FIDE World Championship tied 1-1 in Geneva.
snippets: Sindarov will command the white pieces in Game 3 as both grandmasters eye the 7.5-point title threshold. D Gukesh pulled the emergency brake on Wednesday. Playing with the white pieces in Game 2 of the FIDE World Championship in Geneva, the reigning world champion opted for a rapid three-fold repetition against Uzbekistan's Javokhir Sindarov, shaking hands on a bloodless draw after just 20 moves.

Sindarov held complete parity, leaving Gukesh with zero attacking lanes. Rather than grind through a fruitless middle game, Gukesh steered directly into a repetition of moves. Under FIDE regulations, players cannot agree to a mutual draw before reaching move 40.

Pressured in Tuesday's opener with black, Gukesh reached for the London System to open Game 2—seeking control and a whisper of opening nostalgia. Sindarov refused to blink. The Uzbek grandmaster defused white's setup with clinical symmetry, stripping the position of all tactical bite.

lOExng6l.description: Sindarov admitted afterwards that he had not calculated the consequences of the c4-break precisely, as he felt the position was not yet ripe for such a break. Gukesh astutely added that a draw seemed the natural outcome at that point, since he could not see how either side could achieve anything through a pawn break.
snippets: The game opened with the London System, a solid setup that generally allows both sides to develop their pieces naturally. Gukesh has plenty of experience with this opening from the white side. His most recent success with it dates back to the India–Uzbekistan match at the Olympiad in Samarkand last September, when he defeated Sindarov’s teammate Ortik Nigmatov.

Although Black has several reasonable ways to meet the London System, Sindarov followed the aforementioned game until the sixth move. Both players seemed familiar with the line up to around move 10, when they began spending more time on their decisions. Gukesh gradually arranged his pieces in preparation for the first clash between the two armies.

In retrospect, Gukesh was not disappointed with either the nature or the outcome of the game. At the post-round press conference, he explained that it often happens that Black manages to neutralise White’s opening idea, leaving little room for further progress. So early in the match, he felt there was no reason to take unnecessary risks. Javokhir Sindarov will have the white pieces for the second time in the match tomorrow, when game three is scheduled to take place at 3 p.m.

yXYaH4PC.description: Once again, Gukesh fell behind on the clock, but just when Sindarov had gone for a bold pawn push and action seemed to be heating up, the game ended in a 20-move draw by repetition, leaving the scores level at 1-1.
snippets: Sindarov later explained: "Not about chess, some mental things. Sometimes not even about chess, some other stuff—just to relax before a game and not be nervous." Gukesh arrived with his coach, GM Grzegorz Gajewski.

Gukesh justified his choice as follows: It’s a good opening! And nowadays everything from both colors is so playable; there’s so much to explore because of engines. I don’t think one opening is better than the others. They’re all possible, and I thought it would be a nice, cool way to start the match! I thought it would be a nice, cool way to start the match! ... As in game one, however, it was Sindarov who played faster in the opening, despite admitting to being somewhat surprised: "Actually I was not expecting the London, but I checked this line before also a lot."
The next move to surprise both commentators and Gukesh was 11...Qd8. Sindarov's 11...Qd8!? puzzles our commentators.
